summary: Extend the strong falling-body chapter with a horizontal resistive-force case and parachute-deployment reasoning.

improvements.why: Outcome 9702-3.2.3 says objects moving against a resistive force may reach a terminal constant velocity; the note explains only falling bodies, while the learner's source gives a car driven against friction.
improvements.what: Add a concise horizontal-motion comparison: driving force greater than friction means acceleration, equal forces mean constant velocity, and smaller driving force means deceleration. Include $F_\mathrm{res}=F_\mathrm{drive}-F_\mathrm{friction}$ and a brief numerical example based on a car, paraphrased from the library.

improvements.why: The main bank has one horizontal friction calculation and no item requiring an explanation of the three driving-force regimes.
improvements.what: One Explain structured item comparing acceleration, constant velocity and deceleration for a car as driving force changes relative to friction; one Predict item about a car reaching a constant maximum speed as resistive force grows. Give markable force-resultant reasoning and hints.

improvements.why: The existing main items focus on drag growing during a fall; parachute opening reverses the force imbalance and exposes the common confusion between upward acceleration and upward motion.
improvements.what: One Explain structured item and one graph-based Sketch item for a skydiver opening a parachute while descending: drag temporarily exceeds weight, acceleration is upward while velocity remains downward, then a lower terminal downward velocity is reached. Keep graph qualitative and use permitted command words.
